rnAfter informed consent patient was taken to the operating theatre. Sequential compression device was applied and started on each leg. Next, the left ureteral orifice was identified and intubated initially with a 0.035 sensor guidewire with mild resistance with fragments noted to efflux into the bladder follwed by easing of the resistance with passing the wire. Wire was passed proximaly and advancement into the ureter was stopped at the first sign of tactile resistance. The Wire was then secured in place using a clamp. The cystoscope was removed and a semirigid ureteroscope was then placed into the bladder under vision and the left ureteral orifice was entered and the scope advanced proximally. A small fragment was found and lasered (very soft). The fragment was too small to be extracted. A 0.035 Benston guidewire was then passed into the renal pelvis under vision.

rnA lubricated 11/13F access sheath was then passed over the sensor guidewire carefully into the ureter without difficulty. The sheath was then secured to the patients penile skin with an O chromic suture to avoid displacement.
rnThe flexible ureteroscope was then advanced into the kidney under vision and careful nephroscopy ensued with no additional stones located. Ureteroscopy then ensued as the access sheath was withdrawn with no additional stones found. A ureteral stent was then passed under vision without difficulty. 18F foley catheter was then placed. rnRisks of surgery include anesthetic risks as well as bleeding and infection (which we prepare for by cross matching the patient with screened blood) and giving antibiotics per guidelines before. rnAlternative options to surgery include
rn-Active surveillance: Preserved for people with Very Low risk disease. (defined as PSA<10, PSA Density <0.15, Gleason score â‹œ 6 with no pattern 4 or 5, â‹œ 50% cancer/in any core and â‹œ 2 positive cores (Note NCCN allows â‹œ 3 positive cores) ( In a >10 core biopsy) and clinical stage T1c.)
rnIf patients meet this favorable risk criteria and qualifies for active surveillance (Based on John Hopkins Data:)
rnThere is a low risk(4-6%) of reclassification to high grade (Gleason > or = to 4+3) over the next 15 years

rnThe protocol involves first a restaging biopsy - Which I do at 1 month (up to 30% are found to have more aggressive disease than initially caught on initial biopsy- and therefore no longer qualify for active surveillance). Patients are followed with PSA every six months and DRE and repeat biopsy once yearly. rnReclassifcation (upstaging) definition varies. John hopkins does not rely on PSA per say but instead uses biopsy demonstrated reclassification to Gleason 4 or 5 or increased tumor volume on biopsy as their criteria for reclassification while the Toronto group also use PSA doubling time <3 years or PSA velocity(its important to note however that neither of these have been shown to be associated with biopsy reclassification). PSA doubling time and velocity cannot replace regular biopsy
rnMajor risk associated with this approach are the risks of repeat biopsy (bleeding and infection(increased flouroquinolone resistance))
rn
rn-Surgery (Radical Prostatectomy- Open vs Robotic assisted) without lymph node dissection is an option.
rnThe proven difference between the robotic and the open are the quicker convalescence with robotic surgery with discharge usually the second day after surgery and the lower blood loss (with Open carrying a higher likelihood of blood transfusion). Cancer control, Recovery of erectile function and continence have not been shown to be different.
rnThe major intraoperative complications associated with Radical prostatectomy are bleeding and infection and injury to nearby organs including the rectum, major iliac vessels or nerve during lymphadenectomy. Patient will be crossed and typed for blood and may need to be transfused intraoperatively. The blood is screened for Hepatitis B and C, HIV I and II. The risk of transmission of these is not Zero even after screening but is approximately 1 in millions for HIV and 1 in 100,000 for hepatitis. He will receive perioperative antibiotics to lower risks of surgical site infection.
rnPost radical prostatectomy the expected morbidity is stress incontinence which usually resolves within the first year and erectile dysfunction (this is present in all patients initially but depending on the degree of nerve sparing performed (unilateral, Bilateral, Non-nerve sparing) will or will not return. In his case because of the preexisting ED he will no doubt need assistnace (likely injections to regain erections post op) It is safe to say surgery certainly doesnâ€™t improve erections and erections may never be as good as preop although treatments exist for post prostatectomy ED and include (oral PDE 5 inhibitors, Vacuum erection devices, Injections and lastly penile implants). rnIt is advised usually that surgery be delayed 4-6 weeks after biopsy to allow resolution of inflammation that might make the planes more difficult to separate during surgery.

rnBiochemical recurrence usually happens within a median of 2 years of surgery if at all. From biochemical recurrence to metastatic disease usually takes a median of 8 years and generally from development of metastasis to death is a median of 5 years (that's a 15 year natural history).

rnExternal beam radiation is in the form of Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT). This involves 4-8 weeks of daily treatment with linear accelerator. rnStarted off with explaining the following general :
rn
rnFor clinically localized prostate, there is a > 95% chance of being alive 5 years from time of diagnosis
rnFor localized disease treated with radiation or surgery, 92% of patients are alive at 10 years.
rnFor metastatic disease, 50% of patients with hormone sensitive metastatic disease will live >5 years.
rnProstate cancer generally responds to castration for an average of 2-3 years before castrate resistant prostate cancer develops.
rnOnce the diagnosis of Castrate Resistant Metastatic prostate cancer is made, life expectancy is approximately 18-20 months but can be extended beyond 2 years with newer agents
rn
rnI informed the patient that the prostate biopsy results were positive and that positive biopsy results donâ€™t mean an absence of hope.
rn
rnHe is Clinical stage of T1a, pre-biopsy PSA of 3ng/ml and Gleason score of 3+?4.,
rn
rnOptions in broad categories include observation, active surveillance, surgery or radiation with/without hormones
rn
rn
rn
rnRisks of surgery include anesthetic risks as well as bleeding and infection (which we prepare for by cross matching the patient with screened blood) and giving antibiotics per guidelines before. Also as with any surgery there is risk of injury to nearby organs : In this case, prostate, major blood vessels(iliacs) and nerve (obturator).
rn
rnAlternative options to surgery include
rn-Active surveillance: Preserved for people with Very Low risk disease. (defined as PSA<10, PSA Density <0.15, Gleason score â‹œ 6 with no pattern 4 or 5, â‹œ 50% cancer/in any core and â‹œ 2 positive cores (Note NCCN allows â‹œ 3 positive cores) ( In a >10 core biopsy) and clinical stage T1c.)
rn
rnUnfortunately his preop PSA is discordant with the BIOPSY RESULT. WE MUST THEREFORE FIRST RESTAGE AND REPEAT PSA APRROXIMATELY 6 weeks from the biopsy before this can be considered as an appropriate option for him.
rn
rnIf patients meet this favorable risk criteria and qualifies for active surveillance (Based on John Hopkins Data:)
rnThere is a low risk(4-6%) of reclassification to high grade (Gleason > or = to 4+3) over the next 15 years
rnThere is a low risk (<1%) of death from prostate cancer and metastasis over 15 years.
rnThe protocol involves first a restaging biopsy - Which I do at 1 month (up to 30% are found to have more aggressive disease than initially caught on initial biopsy- and therefore no longer qualify for active surveillance). Patients are followed with PSA every six months and DRE and repeat biopsy once yearly. A multiparametric MRI may also be ordered anterior or aggressive cancer is suspected when PSA increases and systematic prostate biopsies are negative. For patients of african descent- A multiparametric MRI strongly recommended before commencing to make sure there is not more aggressive disease that is missed as this group has high risk of upstaging.
rnReclassifcation (upstaging) definition varies. John hopkins does not rely on PSA per say but instead uses biopsy demonstrated reclassification to Gleason 4 or 5 or increased tumor volume on biopsy as their criteria for reclassification while the Toronto group also use PSA doubling time <3 years or PSA velocity(its important to note however that neither of these have been shown to be associated with biopsy reclassification). PSA doubling time and velocity cannot replace regular biopsy
rnMajor risk associated with this approach are the risks of repeat biopsy (bleeding and infection(increased flouroquinolone resistance))
rn
rn-Surgery (Radical Prostatectomy- Open vs Robotic assisted) with/without lymph node dissection is an option.
rnThe proven difference between the robotic and the open are the quicker convalescence with robotic surgery with discharge usually the second day after surgery and the lower blood loss (with Open carrying a higher likelihood of blood transfusion). Cancer control, Recovery of erectile function and continence have not been shown to be different.
rnThe major intraoperative complications associated with Radical prostatectomy are bleeding and infection and injury to nearby organs including the rectum, major iliac vessels or nerve during lymphadenectomy. Patient will be crossed and typed for blood and may need to be transfused intraoperatively. The blood is screened for Hepatitis B and C, HIV I and II. The risk of transmission of these is not Zero even after screening but is approximately 1 in millions for HIV and 1 in 100,000 for hepatitis. He will receive perioperative antibiotics to lower risks of surgical site infection.
rnPost radical prostatectomy the expected morbidity is stress incontinence which usually resolves within the first year and erectile dysfunction (this is present in all patients initially but depending on the degree of nerve sparing performed (unilateral, Bilateral, Non-nerve sparing) will or will not return. It is safe to say surgery certainly doesnâ€™t improve erections and erections may never be as good as preop although treatments exist for post prostatectomy ED and include (oral PDE 5 inhibitors, Vacuum erection devices, Injections and lastly penile implants). Even after bilateral nerve sparing surgery it may take up to a year or a year and a half to recover maximal erectile function,
rnIt is advised usually that surgery be delayed 4-6 weeks after biopsy to allow resolution of inflammation that might make the planes more difficult to separate during surgery.
rnPost operatively we would be able to do additional prognostication based on surgery pathological findings using normograms. I explained that a PSA would be checked one month after surgery then three monthly and values should ideally be less than 0.02. Biochemical recurrence is usually due to invisible cancerous cells not visible on currently available imaging(MRI/CT, Bone scan etc) that may have left the prostate even before surgery.
rnUnfortunately Robotic Radical prostatectomy is not available in Nigeria but this option may be explored abroad if interested.
rnBiochemical recurrence usually happens within a median of 2 years of surgery if at all. From biochemical recurrence to metastatic disease usually takes a median of 8 years and generally from development of metastasis to death is a median of 5 years (that's a 15 year natural history).
rn
rn-Also they could consider Radiation(Brachytherapy vs External Beam radiation or a combination of both) possibly Hormone therapy (6 months for intermediate risk disease, 3yrs of medical castration for high risk disease). Single modality treatment often adequate for low risk disease.
rnExternal beam radiation is in the form of Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT). This involves 4-8 weeks of daily treatment with linear accelerator. For low and intermediate risk disease the results are equivalent to surgery. For High risk disease there is some data suggesting surgery performs better.
rn
rnIf interested in radiation, given his risk classification he may need to be on Testosterone suppression (medically) for â€¦â€¦ month/yrs in addition. Side effects usually result from inadvertent radiation to close by organs including bowel/bladder with risks of delayed malignancy as a result. Erectile dysfunction resulting from radiation is usually delayed and comes much later compared to surgery.
rnUnfortunately Image Modulated Radiation Therapy is not an option available in Nigeria(although radiation without image guidance is) but can be explored if interested abroad.
rn- The last option would be to do nothing in which case there is risk of metastasis and associated morbidities of bone pain/fractures, spinal compression and paraplegia/inability to walk, hematuria and lower urinary tract symptoms. In someone with otherwise very poor health this could be an option but is not advised in a patient otherwise healthy with a life expectancy >10 years.
rn
rnI have advised that he think about the options while in the meantime we order an MRI of the abdomen/pelvis to rule out soft tissue metastasis and a nuclear bone scan to rule out bone metastasis (Evercare). He will also do a repeat PSA in 2 weeks. (>6 weeks from the biopsy)
rn
rnIf PSA normalizes and he falls into the active surveillance criteria he would still need a confirmatory biopsy to rule out more ominous disease potentially missed at the first biopsy

rn-RE: Surgery (Radical Prostatectomy- Open vs Robotic assisted) with/without lymph node dissection is an option.
rnThe proven difference between the robotic and the open are the quicker convalescence with robotic surgery with discharge usually the second day after surgery and the lower blood loss (with Open carrying a higher likelihood of blood transfusion). Cancer control, Recovery of erectile function and continence have not been shown to be different.
rnThe major intraoperative complications associated with Radical prostatectomy are bleeding and infection and injury to nearby organs including the rectum, major iliac vessels or nerve during lymphadenectomy. Patient will be crossed and typed for blood and may need to be transfused intraoperatively. The blood is screened for Hepatitis B and C, HIV I and II. He will receive perioperative antibiotics to lower risks of surgical site infection.
rnPost radical prostatectomy the expected morbidity is stress incontinence which usually resolves within the first year and erectile dysfunction (this is present in all patients initially but depending on the degree of nerve sparing performed (unilateral, Bilateral, Non-nerve sparing) will or will not return.
